title: MolecularIQ: Symbolic Verification on Molecular Graphs
one_liner: MolecularIQ is a benchmark that tests whether language models can reason over the actual structure of molecules using only tasks whose answers can be computed exactly from the molecular graph.
lead: Today's language models claim to understand chemistry, but most benchmarks test memorized facts rather than real reasoning about how atoms connect. MolecularIQ solves this by creating test tasks where the answer is not somewhere in a training document—it must be computed from scratch using the molecular structure, like counting atoms or finding rings.

problem.h2: Chemistry benchmarks today leak the answers
paras: Current chemistry benchmarks use real-world molecular data downloaded from public sources or textbooks. But those same sources were used to train the language models being tested. So when a model answers correctly, we cannot tell if it truly understands the molecular structure or simply memorized the answer during training.

A beginner might try to test the model on new molecules from the same source. But the model has already learned patterns from thousands of similar examples, so it guesses correctly without reasoning. It is like asking a student a memorized math answer instead of asking them to derive it.

callout.html: Build a benchmark where every answer is computed step-by-step from the molecular graph, so every answer is mathematically verifiable and impossible to have memorized.

steps.text: Feature counting (how many atoms?), index-based attribution (which atoms have this property?), and constrained generation (build a molecule with these properties).
Vary complexity (small to large), task load (single vs. multiple constraints), and representation (different ways to encode the structure).
Use RDKit (an exact molecular chemistry library) to derive the correct answer from each molecule's graph structure.
Run each language model with tailored input formats and extraction methods optimized for that model.
Measure success per task type and complexity, revealing which models truly reason about structure.

paras: Instead of using answers that come from datasets and may appear in training corpora, MolecularIQ uses answers that are computed from the input molecular graph via an algorithmic solver. The ground truth is never looked up—it is generated.

hidden.name: constraint-tracking strength
paras: Constraint-tracking strength is how well a model enforces multiple requirements at once when generating a new molecule. For example, if asked to make a molecule with exactly 5 atoms and at least 2 rings, the model must satisfy both at the same time, not just one or the other.

The paper measures this by examining the success rate on multi-constraint generation tasks (which require 2, 3, or 5 properties to be true simultaneously) and comparing it to single-constraint tasks. If the success rate drops steeply as constraints multiply, the model is not tracking them faithfully.

heat.caption: Darker means higher success rate. Large MoE models handle constraints better than chemistry-tuned models.

reads.html: When a model must satisfy multiple rules at once (like two colors and a size), it either tracks all of them or forgets one partway through. The success rate drops when the number of rules increases.

Multi-constraint generation exposes compositional reasoning: most models score high on single constraints but drop sharply on multi-constraint tasks with 2, 3, or 5 requirements, revealing weak constraint tracking even for top performers.

mechanism.h2: Why symbolic ground truth fixes evaluation
paras: A language model trained on billions of text documents has memorized trillions of facts, including molecular properties. Asking it to answer a question whose answer already exists in its training data is like asking a student on a test if they recognize their own homework—the answer does not prove understanding, only memory.

MolecularIQ breaks this trap by creating tasks where the ground truth never existed in any document. The answer is derived algorithmically from the molecular graph using RDKit, a chemistry software library. The model must actually parse the molecular structure and reason about it, because there is no memorized answer to rely on.

This shift forces the evaluation to measure actual reasoning: the model reads the molecular structure, applies logical operations (count the nitrogen atoms, find atoms with at least 3 bonds, generate structures satisfying constraints), and produces an answer. When the model fails, we know it is a reasoning failure, not a memorization gap.

stages.s: model encodes the structure into a representation it understands
model performs reasoning (count, index, or generate)
RDKit computes the correct answer from the graph independently
answer matches ground truth: true reasoning; answer differs: reasoning failure

math.words: success_rate = (number of models' outputs satisfying all k constraints) / (total test cases) for single vs. multi-constraint generation
symbols: fraction of correct answers on single-constraint tasks (0 to 1)
fraction of correct answers on k-constraint tasks (0 to 1)
how much success falls when constraints multiply (reveals compositional weakness)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Model A on single constraint (make a 5-atom molecule): 80 out of 100 correct. success_single = 0.80.
Model A on two constraints (5 atoms AND 2 rings): 56 out of 100 correct. success_multi-2 = 0.56.
drop_rate = 0.80 - 0.56 = 0.24. The model loses 24 percentage points when asked to track two rules.
Model B on single constraint: 78 correct (0.78). On two constraints: 72 correct (0.72). drop_rate = 0.06.
Model B is much better at compositional reasoning: it only drops 6 points instead of 24.

math.note: A steep drop in success reveals that the model forgets constraints as the problem gets richer, a sign of weak structural reasoning.

bars.h2: Reasoning by model scale and type

charts.title: Chemistry-tuned LLMs (small/specialized)
charts.note: Fine-tuned on chemistry data but weak on compositional reasoning. Knowledge does not carry over when the model encounters unfamiliar combinations of constraints.

charts.title: Large MoE models (generalist, many expert parameters)
charts.note: Larger models and mixture-of-experts routing preserve reasoning capacity across task types and complexity, even without chemistry training.

items.html: Large molecules have many atoms and bonds. A model may track the first two constraints but forget the third when the molecular graph is complex, because it runs out of reasoning capacity mid-calculation.

The model generates a string that looks like molecular notation (SMILES) but is invalid: a bond to a non-existent atom, a ring closure that does not match, or an atom count that violates valency rules. The molecule is uninterpretable.
The model is asked to count atoms or properties exactly (must return 7, not approximately 7). Off-by-one errors or rounding mistakes cause complete failure on counting tasks.

items.b: Done right: model tested on unseen molecules.
items.html: If the model succeeds on MolecularIQ, we know it genuinely parses molecular structure and reasons through constraints, because every task is algorithmically generated and has never appeared in training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should take a small benchmark subset (10-20 molecules with 3 task types: counting, indexing, and constrained generation) and run a language model on it. For each task, measure whether the model's answer matches the RDKit ground truth. Show a per-molecule report: did the model count the atoms correctly? Did it identify all hydrogens? Did it generate a valid molecule satisfying the constraints? Build a simple bar chart showing success rate per task type, and highlight at least one failure case (e.g., model counted 5 atoms but the graph has 7; model forgot the ring constraint and generated an acyclic molecule).
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_per_task = (correct answers on task type) / (total test molecules), breakdown by [counting, indexing, generation]
demo.closing: The demo makes it impossible to miss that reasoning from molecular graph structure is hard, because even large models fail in predictable ways on tasks that were never in their training data—revealing that those failures are genuine reasoning gaps, not memorization gaps.
